etymologies.etymologyHTML: Borrowed from Latin distortum, past participle of distorqueō (“to twist, torture, distort”).

definitions.definition: (transitive) To bring something out of shape, to misshape.

quote.citation: 1902, Hilaire Belloc, The Path to Rome:
quote.text: This she did with the utmost politeness, though cold by race, and through her politeness ran a sense of what the Teutons call Duty, which would once have repelled me; but I have wandered over a great part of the world and I know it now to be a distorted kind of virtue.

definitions.definition: (transitive) To give a false or misleading account of

quote.citation: 1596, Edmund Spenser, “Book V, Canto XII”, in The Faerie Queene. […], London:  […]  [John Wolfe] for William Ponsonbie, →OCLC, stanza 36:
quote.text: Her face was ugly and her mouth distort.
